posts.heading: September 20, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 233 feeder visits and 18 species, slightly busier than the 217 average for the past week. All eleven species recorded on each of the last seven days, including Tufted Titmice, Carolina Chickadees, and Northern Cardinals, were present again.

Tufted Titmice led the count with 113 visits, while Northern Cardinals and Ruby-throated Hummingbirds each accounted for 14. A Tufted Titmouse visited the tube seed feeder, and a female Northern Cardinal perched on the station's metal bar.

Audio detections totaled 334, slightly above the weekly average, driven largely by Carolina Wrens and Northern Cardinals. Northern Mockingbirds, present every day until now, were absent today.

posts.heading: September 19, 2026
posts.text:
The day registered 213 feeder visits and 17 species, placing it above the seven-day average for visits but below it for species counts and audio detections. The 14 species heard fell short of the 287.4 average detections.

Audio activity dropped significantly compared to the previous week, with 223 total detections against the 287.4 average. This reduction corresponds with the shift to the new pi-mic audio source installed on September 13, which replaced the previous c120 unit.

Visual observations captured 12 species across 213 visits. The Tufted Titmouse was the most frequently seen visitor with 101 confident visits, followed by the Carolina Chickadee with 41. A Northern Cardinal provided the day's last visual sighting, occurring 4 minutes before sunset.

posts.heading: September 18, 2026
posts.text:
September 18 added up to a quiet day at the station, with 99 feeder visits significantly below the previous seven-day average of 199.7. The count of 17 species matched the weekly average, but the drop in physical traffic stood out against the 302 visits recorded on Thursday.

The subdued visitation aligns with the installation of a new seed feeder on September 13, which replaced an old unit that was causing bird detection problems. No new species were introduced by the audio switch to the pi-mic on September 13, and the station’s roster remained consistent with the week’s standard residents.

Mourning Doves, a regular presence for the last seven days, were absent today, as were Gray Catbirds and Northern House Wrens. The day closed with a Ruby-throated Hummingbird visiting just six minutes after sunset, marking the final visual record.

posts.heading: September 17, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 302 feeder visits and 19 species, a clear step up from the recent average of 169.4 visits and 14.4 species. This follows a steady climb since September 13, when the audio source was switched to the new microphone and the problematic seed feeder was replaced. Detection counts have risen consistently over the last four days.

Regulars like the Carolina Wren, Tufted Titmouse, and Northern Cardinal held their positions. The Tufted Titmouse led visual visits, appearing 123 times, while the Ruby-throated Hummingbird and House Finch rounded out the top visual feeders. These core species, along with the Blue Jay and Carolina Chickadee, appear on the records every day of the past week.

Newer additions to the week's list included the Eastern Phoebe and American Goldfinch, both of which have only appeared twice in the last seven days. The White-eyed Vireo was also recorded for the second time this week. In contrast, the Pileated Woodpecker and Cedar Waxwing, seen earlier in the period, were absent from the logs today.

posts.heading: September 16, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged 18 species and 244 feeder visits, well above the seven-day average of 13.4 species and 137.7 visits. Regulars including the Tufted Titmouse, Carolina Wren, and Northern Cardinal were heard frequently throughout the day.

Visual observations highlighted the Tufted Titmouse, seen 104 times, and the Ruby-throated Hummingbird, recorded 36 times. The day included the station’s first confident visual record of the Eastern Phoebe. White-eyed Vireo was heard for the first time in the past week, a detection recorded on the new microphone installed earlier this week.

A new seed feeder installed on September 13 replaced an old unit that had caused detection problems. The treat bowl was also refilled with peanuts on September 10.

posts.heading: September 15, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded 18 species and 278 feeder visits, compared to weekly averages of 11.7 and 98.0. Carolina Wren, Carolina Chickadee, and Northern Cardinal were present, as were Tufted Titmouse and Mourning Dove. The Red-shouldered Hawk was absent after appearing on three of the previous seven days.

The switch to the pi-mic audio source on September 13 changed detection capabilities. Cedar Waxwing and Downy Woodpecker were detected once each under the new audio feed.

The Eastern Phoebe marks the station's first confident visual record. The treat bowl, installed earlier in the week, continued to attract crows and other foragers. The upward trend in visits continues since the seed feeder was replaced on September 13.

posts.heading: September 14, 2026
posts.text:
The station recorded its busiest day of the past week, with 241 feeder visits and 15 species against a weekly average of 64 visits and 10 species. Regulars such as the Carolina Wren, Blue Jay, and Eastern Towhee remained present, while the American Goldfinch, Eastern Screech-Owl, and Pileated Woodpecker were absent. The Ruby-throated Hummingbird was first seen 13 minutes after sunrise and last seen at sunset.

The increased activity followed the installation of a new seed feeder on September 13, which replaced a unit causing detection problems. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees contributed to the high visit counts. No new audio detections were attributed to the microphone change, as no new species were heard for the first time.

The day’s totals were driven by consistent feeder use across multiple species, including the Mourning Dove and Northern Cardinal. With no new stations added or removed beyond the seed feeder replacement, the absence of earlier-week outliers confirms this as a peak in the recent seven-day trend.
